etymology: From the Old French atirier, to put in order or array — a, to, and tire, rank or order. Attire is dress considered as an arrangement, a deliberate composition, and therefore always a statement about the wearer’s intent.
biblical_def: Attire in Scripture is never merely covering; it is a declaration, and the three uses of the word show it declaring three different things. It announces a trade: “there met him a woman with the attire of an harlot, and subtil of heart” (Pro 7:10). The young man void of understanding did not need to be told what she was; she had dressed the message, and Solomon puts the attire and the subtil heart in a single breath because the clothing was the first sentence of the argument. It announces a nation’s allure: Oholibah doted on the Chaldeans, “exceeding in dyed attire upon their heads, all of them princes to look to” (Eze 23:15) — Judah seduced by the look of an empire, which is how political idolatry usually begins. And most piercingly, it announces what a woman cannot forget: “Can a maid forget her ornaments, or a bride her attire? yet my people have forgotten me days without number” (Jer 2:32). The comparison is devastating in its ordinariness. No bride mislays her wedding dress; the thing is unthinkable, and the LORD says His people have done the unthinkable with Him — not in a moment of crisis but days without number, by simple, unremarkable forgetting.
webster_summary: Dress considered as an arrangement or array; clothing that declares the wearer’s station, trade, or intent.
webster_full: ATTIRE, n. Dress; clothes; habit; whatever is put on for ornament or defense.
ATTIRE, v.t. To dress; to array; to adorn with garments.
From the Old French atirier, to put in order, from a and tire, order, rank.
In Scripture, dress regarded as a declaration: the attire of an harlot (Pro 7:10).
The head-dress in particular; hence dyed attire upon their heads (Eze 23:15).
scriptures: Pro 7:10
And, behold, there met him a woman with the attire of an harlot, and subtil of heart.
Jer 2:32
Can a maid forget her ornaments, or a bride her attire? yet my people have forgotten me days without number.
Girded with girdles upon their loins, exceeding in dyed attire upon their heads, all of them princes to look to, after the manner of the Babylonians of Chaldea, the land of their nativity:

I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels.
corruption_summary: It is now insisted that clothing carries no message and that to read one is to blame the wearer — a claim Pro 7:10 denies by treating attire as the harlot’s opening argument.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the denial that dress communicates. The modern rule holds that clothing is a purely private matter of taste and comfort, that no inference may be drawn from it, and that to observe an intention behind a garment is to excuse whatever follows. Two things must be said, and the order matters. First, no attire has ever justified a sin committed against the wearer; Scripture lays the guilt of the adulterer squarely on the adulterer, and the man in Pro 7 is not excused for one line — he goes as an ox to the slaughter, and the chapter is a warning to him. Second, and equally, dress is communication, and Scripture treats it as such without embarrassment. The woman of Pro 7 had a costume for her trade; the priest had garments for glory and for beauty; the widow had her weeds; Tamar changed her veil and was taken for another woman.

Recover the plain sense: the question a Christian asks of clothing is not am I permitted but what am I saying, and to whom, and why? Nobody wearing clothes is silent, and the pretence of neutrality merely leaves the message unexamined. Then let Jer 2:32 do the deeper work, because that verse turns the whole subject inward. God does not rebuke Judah’s wardrobe there; He uses the bride’s care for her attire as a rebuke to her carelessness about Him. Whatever we would never forget shows what we actually treasure. The remedy is in Isaiah, who takes the same imagery and puts the best garment on: he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments (Isa 61:10).
roots_summary: Old French atirier, to set in order — dress as arrangement and declaration; the harlot’s costume and the bride’s unforgettable array.
roots_lines: Attire — Old French atirier, to put in order or array.
From a (to) and tire, rank, order — dress as deliberate composition.
Pro 7:10: the attire of an harlot, joined to a subtil heart.
Eze 23:15: dyed attire on Chaldean heads — the look that seduced Judah.
Jer 2:32: no bride forgets her attire, yet God’s people forgot Him days without number.
usage: No attire excuses a sin against the wearer; and no attire is silent.
Jer 2:32 turns the subject inward: what we never forget shows what we treasure.
Isa 61:10 supplies the best garment — the robe of righteousness.

etymology: A shortened form of attire, restricted to the head — a head-dress, turban, or bonnet. The same word gives the tire of a wheel, which is its band or binding; a head-tire is what binds and adorns the head.
biblical_def: A tire is a head-dress, and its single occurrence sits at the centre of the hardest command ever given to a prophet. Ezekiel is told that God will take away the desire of his eyes with a stroke, “yet neither shalt thou mourn nor weep, neither shall thy tears run down” (Eze 24:16), and then: “Forbear to cry, make no mourning for the dead, bind the tire of thine head upon thee, and put on thy shoes upon thy feet, and cover not thy lips” (Eze 24:17). Every item listed is the reversal of a mourning custom. A mourner in Israel bared his head, went barefoot, and covered his upper lip; Ezekiel is ordered to keep his turban bound, keep his shoes on, and leave his face uncovered. Then comes the flattest sentence in the prophets: “So I spake unto the people in the morning: and at even my wife died; and I did in the morning as I was commanded” (Eze 24:18). He preached, she died, he obeyed. The reason given is that Ezekiel is himself a sign: the temple, the desire of Israel’s eyes, was about to fall, and the exiles would be so overwhelmed that ordinary mourning would fail them. The prophet’s bound tire preached what no sermon could. And it is worth noting that God does not call the loss small — He calls her the desire of thine eyes. The cost is named before the command is given.
webster_summary: A head-dress or turban; a contraction of attire restricted to the head, as the tire of a wheel is its binding band.
webster_full: TIRE, n. A head-dress; an ornament for the head; attire.
A contraction of attire, limited in use to the head.
The band or hoop of a wheel; that which binds it together.
TIRE, v.t. To dress or adorn the head (2Ki 9:30, tired her head).
Isa 3:18: the round tires like the moon, crescent ornaments of the daughters of Zion.
scriptures: Son of man, behold, I take away from thee the desire of thine eyes with a stroke: yet neither shalt thou mourn nor weep, neither shall thy tears run down.
Forbear to cry, make no mourning for the dead, bind the tire of thine head upon thee, and put on thy shoes upon thy feet, and cover not thy lips, and eat not the bread of men.
So I spake unto the people in the morning: and at even my wife died; and I did in the morning as I was commanded.
Isa 3:18
In that day the Lord will take away the bravery of their tinkling ornaments about their feet, and their cauls, and their round tires like the moon,
corruption_summary: The passage is cited as evidence of a cruel God demanding suppressed grief, when the text names the loss as the desire of his eyes and makes the prophet’s silence a sermon to a doomed people.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the charge of divine cruelty, and it deserves an honest answer rather than a soft one. God does take Ezekiel’s wife and does forbid him to mourn her publicly, and no amount of explanation makes that an easy chapter. But notice what the text refuses to do. It does not minimise her: she is the desire of thine eyes, named so by God Himself before the stroke falls. It does not pretend Ezekiel felt nothing; the command forbear to cry presumes the crying. And it does not make the loss meaningless: the prophet is told plainly that he is a sign unto the house of Israel, and when they ask wilt thou not tell us what these things are to us? the explanation is given.

Recover the plain sense: prophets in Scripture do not merely deliver messages, they become them. Hosea married Gomer, Isaiah walked naked and barefoot three years, Jeremiah wore a yoke and buried a girdle, and Ezekiel lay on his side for months, cooked over dung, and now buries his wife dry-eyed. This is costly and it is not arbitrary — God spends His servants to reach a people who will not hear words. It also stands as an unanswerable rebuke to any ministry conducted at no personal expense. Note finally that Ezekiel is forbidden the customs of mourning, not the grief itself, and that the God who required this of him is the God who wept at a grave Himself before He opened it.
roots_summary: A contraction of attire, restricted to the head — the turban Ezekiel was commanded to keep bound the day his wife died.
roots_lines: Tire — shortened from attire; a head-dress or turban.
The same word gives the tire of a wheel — its binding band.
Eze 24:17: binding the tire and keeping the shoes on reverse the mourning customs.
A mourner bared his head, went barefoot, and covered his upper lip.
Isa 3:18: round tires like the moon, crescent head-ornaments.
usage: Every item in Eze 24:17 is the reversal of an Israelite mourning custom.
God names the loss the desire of thine eyes before He commands the silence.
Ezekiel is forbidden the customs of mourning, not the grief.

etymology: From the Old French bracel, a little arm-band, diminutive of the Latin brachium, the arm. Ornaments for the wrist or arm; in Scripture frequently gifts of betrothal, and once a pledge given in shame.
biblical_def: Bracelets in Scripture are tokens, and everything depends on who gives them and why. At the well of Nahor, Abraham’s servant, having seen his prayer answered before he had finished praying it, “took a golden earring of half a shekel weight, and two bracelets for her hands of ten shekels weight of gold” (Gen 24:22). They are the earnest of a betrothal, given before Rebekah knows the errand, and Laban’s eye lights on them at once — “when he saw the earring and bracelets upon his sister’s hands” (Gen 24:30), a detail the narrator includes without comment and which tells us a great deal about Laban. In Judah’s squalid transaction with Tamar the bracelets go the other way: “Thy signet, and thy bracelets, and thy staff that is in thine hand” (Gen 38:18) — a pledge handed over in a moment of appetite and produced months later as evidence, so that a man’s own ornaments convict him. And in Ezekiel they become the emblem of covenant grace: “I decked thee also with ornaments, and I put bracelets upon thy hands, and a chain on thy neck” (Eze 16:11). Jerusalem is a foundling in a field, unwashed and cast out, and God clothes and jewels her as a bride — which makes the chapter’s later account of her whoredoms all the more terrible, since she took the very jewels He gave and spent them on idols.
webster_summary: Ornaments for the wrist or arm; in Scripture tokens of betrothal, pledges of debt, and the emblems of covenant grace bestowed on an unloved bride.
webster_full: BRACELET, n. An ornament for the wrist; a band or chain worn about the arm.
From the Old French bracel, diminutive of Latin brachium, the arm.
Anciently a piece of defensive armour for the arm.
In Scripture, given as betrothal gifts (Gen 24:22) and as pledges (Gen 38:18).
Figuratively, of the ornaments with which God decks His covenant people (Eze 16:11).
scriptures: And it came to pass, as the camels had done drinking, that the man took a golden earring of half a shekel weight, and two bracelets for her hands of ten shekels weight of gold;

And I asked her, and said, Whose daughter art thou? And she said, The daughter of Bethuel, Nahor's son, whom Milcah bare unto him: and I put the earring upon her face, and the bracelets upon her hands.
And he said, What pledge shall I give thee? And she said, Thy signet, and thy bracelets, and thy staff that is in thine hand. And he gave it her, and came in unto her, and she conceived by him.
I decked thee also with ornaments, and I put bracelets upon thy hands, and a chain on thy neck.
corruption_summary: Eze 16 is avoided as too coarse for public reading, which loses the Bible’s most graphic account of grace — a castaway infant washed, clothed, jewelled, and married by God.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the sanitising of the covenant story. Ezekiel 16 is rarely read aloud and rarely preached, because it is frank in a way modern congregations find uncomfortable: an abandoned newborn in a field, unwashed, unsalted, unswaddled, left to die; God passing by and saying Live; the child growing, and God spreading His skirt over her and entering into covenant with her; then the clothing, the broidered work, the silk, the jewels, the bracelets, the crown. And then her prostitution, in language that spares nothing. Skip the chapter and you lose the most detailed picture Scripture gives of what grace actually is — not the rewarding of a promising candidate but the rescue of something nobody wanted.

Recover the plain sense: the bracelets are the point of the indictment. God says explicitly that she took His jewels and made images of them, took His broidered garments and covered idols with them, took His oil and His incense and set them before other gods. That is the anatomy of every believer’s besetting sin — the gifts of God turned into instruments against Him. Health, money, intellect, influence, even doctrine and gifts of ministry, are the ornaments He put on our hands, and each may be spent on an idol. And the chapter does not end in the field where it began: God says I will establish unto thee an everlasting covenant, that she may remember and be confounded, and never open her mouth any more because of her shame, when He is pacified toward her for all that she hath done.
roots_summary: Latin brachium, the arm — arm-ornaments; betrothal tokens at a well, a pledge in shame, and the jewels of covenant grace.
roots_lines: Bracelets — Old French bracel, from Latin brachium, the arm.
Anciently also a piece of armour for the forearm.
Gen 24:22: the betrothal earnest given to Rebekah at the well.
Gen 38:18: Judah’s pledge to Tamar, later produced as evidence against him.
Eze 16:11: the ornaments with which God decked the foundling bride.
usage: Gen 24:30 notes Laban seeing the gold before he greets the man — character in a detail.
Judah’s bracelets convict him: a pledge given in appetite, produced in court.
Eze 16 shows the gifts of God spent upon idols — the anatomy of besetting sin.

etymology: The old plural of hose, from the Saxon hosa — a covering for the legs, and by extension breeches or trousers. The form hosen is the older plural, as oxen to ox.
biblical_def: Hosen occurs once, and the verse is a masterpiece of deliberate detail: “Then these men were bound in their coats, their hosen, and their hats, and their other garments, and were cast into the midst of the burning fiery furnace” (Dan 3:21). Why does the Holy Ghost trouble to itemise the wardrobe of three men about to be burned? Because of what is said thirty verses later, when the princes and governors gather to inspect them: the fire had no power upon their bodies, “nor was an hair of their head singed, neither were their coats changed, nor the smell of fire had passed on them” (Dan 3:27). The clothing is listed going in so that it may be checked coming out. Even the smell was absent. Only one thing burned in that furnace, and Nebuchadnezzar himself reports it: “Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt” (Dan 3:25) — they went in bound, and the ropes were all that the flames consumed. Note also the ground of their courage, spoken before the deliverance and not after: our God is able to deliver us, but if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods. Their obedience did not depend on the outcome, which is why it is worth imitating.
webster_summary: The old plural of hose: coverings for the legs, breeches. Itemised among the garments of the three Hebrews cast into the furnace, so that their preservation might be verified.
webster_full: HOSE, n. A covering for the legs; stockings; breeches.
HOSEN, the old plural, as oxen from ox.
From the Saxon hosa; German Hose, breeches.
Dan 3:21 lists coats, hosen, hats, and other garments.
Dan 3:27 verifies that not one of them was changed, nor the smell of fire upon them.
scriptures: Dan 3:17
If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king.
Dan 3:21
Then these men were bound in their coats, their hosen , and their hats, and their other garments, and were cast into the midst of the burning fiery furnace.
Dan 3:25
He answered and said, Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt; and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God.
Dan 3:27

And the princes, governors, and captains, and the king's counsellors, being gathered together, saw these men, upon whose bodies the fire had no power, nor was an hair of their head singed, neither were their coats changed, nor the smell of fire had passed on them.
corruption_summary: The narrative is preached as a promise that faith secures rescue, which quietly deletes the three men’s own but if not — the clause that makes their stand worth anything.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the deliverance-guaranteed reading. Daniel 3 is a favourite text for teaching that God will rescue those who stand firm, and the furnace is presented as proof that faithfulness is always vindicated in this life. The three Hebrews themselves refuse that theology in the moment of testing. Our God whom we serve is able to deliver us — and then, without pause, but if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up. They stated in advance that their obedience did not depend on being spared. Strip that clause out and the story becomes a transaction: stand firm and you will be rescued. Leave it in, and it becomes a doctrine of God worth dying for.

Recover the plain sense: the God who delivered these three did not deliver James from Herod’s sword, and the same chapter of Hebrews that tells of those who quenched the violence of fire tells also of those who were sawn asunder and of whom the world was not worthy. Both are faith. What Daniel 3 does prove is that the Lord is with His people in the fire — a fourth figure walking loose in the flames — and that what burns is the bindings. Nebuchadnezzar saw men loose, which they had not been when they went in. Sometimes the fire is how God unties a man.
roots_summary: Saxon hosa, leg-coverings — the old plural; itemised entering the furnace so the miracle could be verified leaving it.
roots_lines: Hosen — old plural of hose; Saxon hosa, a leg-covering.
Formed as oxen from ox; the modern plural is hose.
Dan 3:21 lists the garments going in; Dan 3:27 checks them coming out.
Not a hair singed, not a coat changed, not the smell of fire upon them.
Dan 3:25: they went in bound and were seen walking loose.
usage: The wardrobe is itemised so the preservation can be verified in detail.
The ropes were the only thing the fire consumed.
Dan 3:17–18: but if not is the clause that makes the stand worth imitating.

etymology: From the Saxon wencle, a child or young girl, related to wancol, weak or tottering. In 1611 the word carried no reproach whatever: it meant simply a young woman, commonly a servant girl. Its later coarsening is a change in English, not in Scripture.
biblical_def: The wench appears once, in the network of couriers that saved David’s life: “Now Jonathan and Ahimaaz stayed by Enrogel; for they might not be seen to come into the city: and a wench went and told them; and they went and told king David” (2Sa 17:17). The chain is worth tracing. Hushai overturns Ahithophel’s counsel in Absalom’s council; he sends word to Zadok and Abiathar the priests; they send this servant girl out to the spring at Enrogel, because two grown men could not be seen entering the city; she carries the message to Jonathan and Ahimaaz; they run to David; David crosses Jordan by morning, and not one is left behind. Absalom’s men pursue, and a woman at Bahurim hides the messengers in a well and spreads ground corn over its mouth (2Sa 17:18–20), lying to the pursuers with perfect composure. The deliverance of the LORD’s anointed ran that night through two unnamed women and a covered well. Scripture is full of such links. The narrative never pauses to praise the girl and never gives her a name, and the kingdom of Judah turns on her errand as surely as on Hushai’s eloquence in the council chamber.
webster_summary: A young woman, especially a servant girl; in 1611 an entirely respectful word, since coarsened in English but not in Scripture.
webster_full: WENCH, n. A young woman; a girl; a maiden.
From the Saxon wencle, a child, a maid; allied to wancol, tender, weak.
In the older usage a term of no disrespect; commonly a young female servant.
In later English degraded to signify a woman of loose character.
2Sa 17:17: the wench who carried the message from the priests to David’s couriers.
scriptures: Now Jonathan and Ahimaaz stayed by Enrogel; for they might not be seen to come into the city: and a wench went and told them; and they went and told king David.
Nevertheless a lad saw them, and told Absalom: but they went both of them away quickly, and came to a man's house in Bahurim, which had a well in his court; whither they went down.

And when Absalom's servants came to the woman to the house, they said, Where is Ahimaaz and Jonathan? And the woman said unto them, They be gone over the brook of water. And when they had sought and could not find them, they returned to Jerusalem.

And Absalom and all the men of Israel said, The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel. For the LORD had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, to the intent that the LORD might bring evil upon Absalom.
corruption_summary: The word’s coarsening in modern English is offered as evidence that the Authorized Version is crude or demeaning, when the change happened in the language centuries after the translation.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is anachronism — reading a word’s later career back into an older text. Wench in 1611 meant a girl, and could be used of a daughter of the house without the least disrespect; it acquired its coarse sense long afterward. The same has happened to a good many words in the Authorized Version. Let once meant to hinder, prevent to go before, conversation a manner of life, meat any food, suffer to allow. To charge the translators with crudity here is like charging a map with error because the roads have been renamed. It is a reason to learn the older English, not to disparage those who wrote it.

Recover the plain sense: this is the ordinary discipline of reading any old book honestly, and Scripture rewards it. And the verse itself repays the attention, for it records something the Bible does constantly and readers constantly miss — the decisive service rendered by a person the narrative does not bother to name. Hushai’s counsel was defeated in the council chamber because the LORD had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel (2Sa 17:14), and the appointment was executed by a servant girl walking to a spring and a housewife at Bahurim spreading corn over a well. Providence habitually runs through such hands. The people whose obedience carries a kingdom are rarely the people whose names it remembers.
roots_summary: Saxon wencle, a girl — a servant maid; the unnamed messenger through whom David’s escape ran.
roots_lines: Wench — Saxon wencle, a child or young girl.
In 1611 a wholly respectful word for a young woman or maidservant.
Its coarse modern sense developed long after the translation.
2Sa 17:17: she carries word from the priests because the men could not be seen.
2Sa 17:14 gives the true cause: the LORD had appointed to defeat Ahithophel’s counsel.
usage: A dated word is a reason to learn older English, not to disparage the translators.
Compare let (hinder), prevent (go before), conversation (manner of life).
The rescue of the LORD’s anointed ran through two unnamed women.

etymology: From the Saxon cymlic, becoming or seemly, related to become — that which is fitting, graceful, and proper to its object. Comeliness is not mere prettiness but propriety: the beauty of a thing being what it ought to be.
biblical_def: Comeliness is fitting beauty, and Scripture’s uses of it converge on a single startling place. Ezekiel tells Jerusalem that her renown went forth among the heathen for her beauty, “for it was perfect through my comeliness, which I had put upon thee” (Eze 16:14) — a borrowed loveliness, lent and not owned. Daniel, seeing the great vision, reports that “my comeliness was turned in me into corruption, and I retained no strength” (Dan 10:8); the sight of glory undoes a man’s own dignity. And then Isaiah, of the Servant: “he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him” (Isa 53:2). The One who put comeliness upon Jerusalem had none Himself. That is the exchange the chapter goes on to describe in every other particular — He bore our griefs, He was wounded for our transgressions, the chastisement of our peace was upon Him — and the beauty is part of the transaction. Paul completes the doctrine at the level of the body: “those members of the body, which we think to be less honourable, upon these we bestow more abundant honour; and our uncomely parts have more abundant comeliness” (1Co 12:23). God’s way with beauty is to put it where men would not.
webster_summary: Fitting or becoming beauty; grace and propriety rather than mere attractiveness. Bestowed by God on His people, absent from His Servant, and given by Him to the parts men count least.
webster_full: COMELINESS, n. That which is becoming, fit, or suitable; grace; beauty; dignity.
From comely; Saxon cymlic, becoming, seemly, allied to become.
Distinguished from beauty: comeliness is propriety and fitness rather than mere form.
Applied to conduct as well as appearance; that which is seemly in a person’s station.
Isa 53:2: he hath no form nor comeliness, said of the suffering Servant.
scriptures: Isa 53:2
For he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him.
And thy renown went forth among the heathen for thy beauty: for it was perfect through my comeliness, which I had put upon thee, saith the Lord GOD.
Dan 10:8
Therefore I was left alone, and saw this great vision, and there remained no strength in me: for my comeliness was turned in me into corruption, and I retained no strength.
And those members of the body, which we think to be less honourable, upon these we bestow more abundant honour; and our uncomely parts have more abundant comeliness.
corruption_summary: Appearance has become a currency by which people are ranked and valued, which is exactly the scale Isa 53:2 refuses — the Redeemer had nothing on it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the tyranny of appearance. Every age has valued beauty; ours has industrialised it, measuring, ranking, and rewarding it at a scale no previous generation could manage, and training people from childhood to regard their own faces as assets to be optimised. The gospel strikes at this from an unexpected direction. It does not chiefly say that inner beauty matters more, true as that is. It says that when God came to save, He came without any of it: no form nor comeliness, no beauty that we should desire him. The most important Person who ever lived would not have been ranked at all, and if the scale cannot register Him the scale is worthless.

Recover the plain sense: comeliness in Scripture is bestowed, not possessed. Jerusalem’s was my comeliness, which I had put upon thee — loveliness on loan, which she then prostituted. Daniel’s own comeliness turned to corruption the moment he saw real glory, which is what happens to every human excellence brought near the throne. And Paul’s rule for the body settles how the church should behave: the parts we think less honourable receive more abundant honour, and the uncomely parts more abundant comeliness — God deliberately compensating where men would discount. A congregation ordered on that principle looks nothing like the world’s ranking, and is meant not to.
roots_summary: Saxon cymlic, becoming — fitting beauty; lent to Jerusalem, absent from the Servant, given to the parts men count least.
roots_lines: Comeliness — Saxon cymlic, seemly, becoming; allied to become.
Propriety and fitness rather than mere attractiveness of form.
Eze 16:14: my comeliness, which I had put upon thee — beauty on loan.
Dan 10:8: a man’s comeliness turns to corruption before true glory.
Isa 53:2: the Servant had no form nor comeliness at all.
usage: If the scale of appearance cannot register Christ, the scale is worthless.
All human comeliness in Scripture is bestowed, and is undone before glory.
1Co 12:23: God gives more abundant comeliness where men give least honour.

etymology: From the Saxon deorling, a little dear one — deore, dear, with the diminutive -ling. In the Authorized Version it renders the Hebrew yachid, meaning only one or solitary, the same word used of Isaac as Abraham’s only son.
biblical_def: Darling is a term of endearment in modern English and something quite different in the Psalms. It twice renders the Hebrew yachid, the only one, and in both places the psalmist uses it of his own soul: “Deliver my soul from the sword; my darling from the power of the dog” (Psa 22:20), and “rescue my soul from their destructions, my darling from the lions” (Psa 35:17). The parallelism is exact — my soul answers to my darling — and the sense is not sentimental but arithmetical: the soul is a man’s only one. He has one body and may lose parts of it; he has one life and one soul, and there is no second. That is why the plea is so urgent and why our Lord’s question lands where it does: what shall a man give in exchange for his soul? There is nothing to exchange, because it is the only one he has. The setting of Psa 22 makes the word weightier still. This is the psalm that opens My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me, that describes pierced hands and feet and parted garments, and the very next verse cries “Save me from the lion’s mouth: for thou hast heard me” (Psa 22:21). The prayer for the yachid is on the lips of the only begotten Son.
webster_summary: A dearly loved one; in the Psalms rendering the Hebrew for only one, used by the psalmist of his own soul as the single life he possesses.
webster_full: DARLING, n. One much beloved; a favorite.
From the Saxon deorling, from deore, dear, with the diminutive termination -ling.
DARLING, adj. Dearly beloved; regarded with great affection.
In Psa 22:20 and 35:17 it renders the Hebrew yachid, only, solitary.
The same Hebrew is used of Isaac, Abraham’s only son (Gen 22:2).
scriptures: Deliver my soul from the sword; my darling from the power of the dog.
Save me from the lion's mouth: for thou hast heard me from the horns of the unicorns.
Lord, how long wilt thou look on? rescue my soul from their destructions, my darling from the lions.
Gen 22:2

And he said, Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest, and get thee into the land of Moriah; and offer him there for a burnt offering upon one of the mountains which I will tell thee of.
corruption_summary: The soul is treated as one component of a person among many — a dimension to be balanced against career, body, and relationships — where Scripture calls it the only one, with nothing to set beside it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the demotion of the soul to one item on a list. Modern speech divides a person into domains — physical, mental, emotional, financial, social, and somewhere among them the spiritual — and counsels balance among them, as though the soul were a sector requiring its due share of attention. The Hebrew behind darling refuses the arithmetic. Yachid means the only one. A man may lose his health and live, lose his money and live, lose his reputation and live; he has exactly one soul, and its loss is not a setback in one area but the end of him.

Recover the plain sense: our Lord put the whole matter into a question no one has answered — what shall a man give in exchange for his soul? The form of the question is the argument. An exchange requires something of comparable value to offer, and there is nothing, because whatever a man might offer belongs to the same short life he is trying to save. Then observe where the word sits in Psa 22. The psalm of the crucifixion, quoted by Christ from the cross, contains this prayer for the only one — and the same Hebrew describes Isaac bound on Moriah, the only son whom the father loved. Two only sons on two mountains, and on the second the ram did not appear.
roots_summary: Saxon deorling, a little dear one — rendering Hebrew yachid, the only one; the soul as a man’s single, unexchangeable life.
roots_lines: Darling — Saxon deorling, from deore, dear.
Renders the Hebrew yachid, only, solitary, an only child.
Set in parallel with my soul in both Psa 22:20 and Psa 35:17.
The same Hebrew describes Isaac, Abraham’s only son (Gen 22:2).
Psa 22 is the psalm of the crucifixion, quoted by Christ from the cross.
usage: The sense is not sentimental but arithmetical — the soul is the only one.
What shall a man give in exchange for his soul? — there is nothing to offer.
Two only sons on two mountains; on Calvary no ram was provided.

etymology: From the Saxon cleofan, to split — the past participle of cleave in its dividing sense. A cleft is a split, fissure, or crack; as an adjective, divided. English confusingly holds two verbs cleave, one meaning to split apart and one to stick fast, and this word belongs to the first.
biblical_def: A cleft is a split, and Scripture uses it at three very different scales. In the law it is anatomical and defining: “every beast that parteth the hoof, and cleaveth the cleft into two claws, and cheweth the cud among the beasts, that ye shall eat” (Deu 14:6). Two marks were required together, and the double test is instructive — the divided hoof, visible in the animal’s walk, and the chewing of the cud, its inward work. Neither alone sufficed; the camel chewed and did not divide, the swine divided and did not chew. In the prophets the scale is geological: “the mountains shall be molten under him, and the valleys shall be cleft, as wax before the fire” (Mic 1:4), the earth itself splitting at the approach of God. And in the clefts of the rocks men hide: “To go into the clefts of the rocks, and into the tops of the ragged rocks, for fear of the LORD, and for the glory of his majesty” (Isa 2:21) — terror driving men into the stone. Yet the same clefts are a place of safety and of love: “O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the secret places of the stairs, let me see thy countenance” (Son 2:14). Two men in a cleft of the same rock: one hiding from God’s face, one called to show his.
webster_summary: A split, fissure, or crack; as an adjective, divided. Used of the parted hoof, of valleys split before God, and of the rock-clefts men hide in.
webster_full: CLEFT, pp. of cleave; divided; split; parted asunder.
CLEFT, n. A space or opening made by splitting; a crevice; a fissure.
From the Saxon cleofan, to split, to divide.
To be distinguished from the other verb cleave, Saxon clifian, to adhere or stick fast.
Deu 14:6: the beast that cleaveth the cleft into two claws — the divided hoof.
scriptures: Deu 14:6
And every beast that parteth the hoof, and cleaveth the cleft into two claws, and cheweth the cud among the beasts, that ye shall eat.
Mic 1:4
And the mountains shall be molten under him, and the valleys shall be cleft, as wax before the fire, and as the waters that are poured down a steep place.
Isa 2:21
To go into the clefts of the rocks, and into the tops of the ragged rocks, for fear of the LORD, and for the glory of his majesty, when he ariseth to shake terribly the earth.
Son 2:14
O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the secret places of the stairs, let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely.
corruption_summary: The clean-beast test required two marks together — the visible walk and the inward chewing — and every counterfeit of Christian profession fails by keeping one and dropping the other.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The abiding use of the divided hoof is diagnostic. The law required two signs in the same animal: a parted hoof, which shows in how the creature walks and is visible to any observer, and the chewing of the cud, which is inward, slow, and repeated. The camel and the coney chewed but did not divide; the swine divided but did not chew. Neither was clean. Read as the older writers read it, this is a picture of profession and practice, of inward meditation and outward walk, and it exposes both counterfeits at once. There is the man whose conduct is faultless and whose inner life is empty of the word, and the man who ruminates endlessly on doctrine and whose walk is undivided from the world’s.

Recover the plain sense: neither mark alone was ever sufficient, and God appointed the double test because either can be counterfeited by itself. The cud is the man in Psa 1 whose delight is in the law of the LORD and who meditates in it day and night; the parted hoof is the same man who walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly. Then take the clefts as the gospel comfort behind the warning. Men will one day call on the rocks to hide them from the face of Him that sitteth on the throne, and the rocks will not help them; but the Bridegroom calls His dove out of the clefts to show her face, and Moses was hidden in a clift of the rock while the glory passed by. The rock is the same. What differs is whether one is hiding from God or hidden by Him.
roots_summary: Saxon cleofan, to split — a fissure; the parted hoof, the split valleys, and the rock-cleft that hides or shelters.
roots_lines: Cleft — Saxon cleofan, to split; past participle of cleave (to divide).
Distinct from the other cleave (Saxon clifian), to stick fast.
Deu 14:6: the cleft hoof, one of two marks required together.
Mic 1:4: valleys cleft as wax before the fire at God’s approach.
Isa 2:21 and Son 2:14: the same rock-clefts hide the terrified and shelter the beloved.
usage: Two marks were required together; the camel chewed without dividing, the swine divided without chewing.
The parted hoof is the visible walk; the cud is the inward meditation.
Isa 2:21 hides men from God; Son 2:14 calls the beloved out of the same clefts.

etymology: From be and the Saxon stede, a place or stead — to be placed, situated, or circumstanced. Hardly bestead means hard-placed, in sore straits; the word describes a man’s position rather than his feelings.
biblical_def: The word occurs once, and its setting is one of the darkest passages in Isaiah: “And they shall pass through it, hardly bestead and hungry: and it shall come to pass, that when they shall be hungry, they shall fret themselves, and curse their king and their God, and look upward” (Isa 8:21). To be hardly bestead is to be hard-placed — not merely distressed in feeling but cornered in circumstance. And Isaiah traces exactly what such men do. They fret; they curse their king and their God; they look upward, and then look to the earth, and behold “trouble and darkness, dimness of anguish; and they shall be driven to darkness” (Isa 8:22). It is a portrait of misery without repentance, and the cause is stated a few verses earlier. The people had been consulting “them that have familiar spirits, and unto wizards that peep, and that mutter” instead of their God, and the prophet lays down the rule that governs the whole passage: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). That is the sentence the hard-placed man most needs. Circumstances cornered them; the darkness came from having sought light where there was none, and no amount of hunger will teach a man anything if he curses upward instead of turning.
webster_summary: Placed or circumstanced; in the phrase hardly bestead, hard-placed, in sore straits and without resource.
webster_full: BESTEAD, v.t. To accommodate; to place; to dispose; to circumstance.
From be and stead; Saxon stede, a place, a station.
Hardly bestead: hard-placed; in difficulty; distressed for want of resource.
Also, to profit or avail; as, it shall little bestead him.
Isa 8:21 is the sole occurrence in the Authorized Version.
scriptures: Isa 8:19
And when they shall say unto you, Seek unto them that have familiar spirits, and unto wizards that peep, and that mutter: should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Isa 8:21
And they shall pass through it, hardly bestead and hungry: and it shall come to pass, that when they shall be hungry, they shall fret themselves, and curse their king and their God, and look upward.
Isa 8:22
And they shall look unto the earth; and behold trouble and darkness, dimness of anguish; and they shall be driven to darkness.
corruption_summary: Guidance is sought today from every source except the one Isaiah names, and the mediums that peep and mutter have simply changed costume — the horoscope, the medium, the manifestation, the inner voice treated as revelation.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is divination in modern dress. Isa 8:19 describes a people consulting those that have familiar spirits, and wizards that peep, and that mutter — a wonderfully contemptuous phrase for the theatrical half-whisper of the professional medium. The prophet’s objection is not that such practitioners fail to entertain but that a nation is enquiring of the dead on behalf of the living while its own God is available and speaking. The present forms are everywhere: the daily horoscope read half in jest, the tarot spread, the medium’s stage show, the manifesting of desired outcomes, and, within the church, the treatment of impressions and hunches as though they were revelation with the authority of Scripture.

Recover the plain sense: Isaiah gives the church its permanent test in one clause — to the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them. The standard is the written word, and it applies to the medium and to the preacher alike. What follows in verse 21 is the sober consequence: men who sought light where there was none end hard-placed, hungry, cursing upward. Note that their trouble is genuine; Isaiah does not mock their hunger. But affliction alone converts nobody — the same hunger that drives one man to his knees drives another to curse his king and his God. The difference is not the severity of the circumstance but whether there is any light in the man to see it by.
roots_summary: Saxon stede, a place — to be placed or circumstanced; hardly bestead is hard-placed, cornered without resource.
roots_lines: Bestead — be + Saxon stede, a place or station.
Hardly bestead describes position, not merely feeling: hard-placed.
A second sense, now obsolete: to avail or profit.
Isa 8:21 is the only occurrence in the Authorized Version.
Isa 8:20 supplies the passage’s rule: to the law and to the testimony.
usage: Isa 8:19 mocks the medium’s theatrical whisper — those that peep, and that mutter.
The darkness follows from seeking light where there was none.
Hunger drives one man to his knees and another to curse upward.

etymology: From the Norse lopt, air, sky, or an upper room — the same root as aloft and lofty. A loft is the upper chamber of a house, reached by an outside stair; in the East, the guest room and the place of retirement.
biblical_def: The loft is an upper room, and both places where the word appears are rooms in which a dead young man was raised. At Zarephath the widow’s son dies, and Elijah says, “Give me thy son. And he took him out of her bosom, and carried him up into a loft, where he abode, and laid him upon his own bed” (1Ki 17:19). He carries the boy up to the room the widow had given him, stretches himself upon the child three times, and cries unto the LORD (1Ki 17:21) — and “the LORD heard the voice of Elijah; and the soul of the child came into him again, and he revived” (1Ki 17:22). The first resurrection recorded in Scripture happens in a spare room over a poor woman’s house in a foreign town, in the middle of a famine. Centuries later, at Troas, “there sat in a window a certain young man named Eutychus, being fallen into a deep sleep: and as Paul was long preaching, he sunk down with sleep, and fell down from the third loft, and was taken up dead” (Act 20:9). Paul goes down, falls on him, embraces him, and says, “Trouble not yourselves; for his life is in him” (Act 20:10) — then goes back up, breaks bread, and talks until daybreak. Two lofts, two young men, two servants of God stretched upon a corpse, and in both cases the life given back through a man lying full length upon the dead.
webster_summary: An upper room or chamber, especially one reached by an outside stair; the guest-chamber of an eastern house.
webster_full: LOFT, n. The upper room or floor of a house or other building.
From the Norse lopt, the air, the sky, an upper chamber; whence aloft, lofty.
In eastern houses, the chamber upon the roof, often set apart for a guest (2Ki 4:10).
A gallery raised within a building; as an organ loft.
Act 20:9: Eutychus fell from the third loft — the third storey.
scriptures: And he said unto her, Give me thy son. And he took him out of her bosom, and carried him up into a loft, where he abode, and laid him upon his own bed.
And he stretched himself upon the child three times, and cried unto the LORD, and said, O LORD my God, I pray thee, let this child's soul come into him again.
And the LORD heard the voice of Elijah; and the soul of the child came into him again, and he revived.
Act 20:9

And there sat in a window a certain young man named Eutychus, being fallen into a deep sleep: and as Paul was long preaching, he sunk down with sleep, and fell down from the third loft, and was taken up dead.
corruption_summary: The Eutychus account is told almost entirely as a joke about long sermons, which buries a resurrection and the plain fact that the church stayed until daybreak.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The distortion here is trivialisation. Act 20:9 is one of the best-known verses in Acts and is quoted almost exclusively as a quip — the man who died of a long sermon — which is amusing precisely once and has cost the passage its weight. A young man fell three storeys and was taken up dead. An apostle raised him. And the assembly, having seen a resurrection, went back upstairs, broke bread, and continued talking until break of day. That is the detail worth noticing, and it is the one the joke buries: nobody went home.

Recover the plain sense: set the two lofts side by side and the same pattern appears in both. Elijah stretched himself upon the child three times; Paul fell on Eutychus and embraced him. In neither case is there a formula or a gesture of power at a distance — the man of God lies down full length upon the dead, identifying himself with the corpse, and God gives the life. It is a picture of the whole ministry, and finally of Christ, who did not raise us from a safe height but came down and joined Himself to our death. Note too where these things happen: a spare room over a widow’s house in a famine, and a crowded third-floor chamber at midnight with too many lamps. God’s great works in Scripture take place in remarkably ordinary rooms.
roots_summary: Norse lopt, an upper room — the guest-chamber; the two rooms in which a young man was raised from the dead.
roots_lines: Loft — Norse lopt, air or upper chamber; whence aloft and lofty.
In eastern houses, the chamber on the roof, often the guest room (2Ki 4:10).
1Ki 17:19: Elijah carries the widow’s dead son up to his own bed.
Act 20:9: Eutychus falls from the third loft — the third storey.
In both, the man of God stretches himself upon the dead.
usage: The first resurrection in Scripture occurs in a spare room in a famine.
Elijah stretched himself three times; Paul fell on him and embraced him.
After the raising at Troas the church stayed and talked until daybreak.
